name: PT Buyung Poetra Sembada Tbk

frontmatter.title: Buyung Poetra — a rice miller priced as a securities portfolio
frontmatter.summary: HOKI trades at Rp32 for a rice business that has not earned a clean operating profit in two years and a securities book that does not cover its bank debt. At the last clean gross margin our DCF values the operating business below zero and the equity at Rp0; the probability-weighted target is Rp4, a -86.3% return. SELL.
thesis: The market is not paying for rice: at IDR309.7bn it is paying for the IDR261.1bn securities book, IDR9.4bn of cash and the IDR13.3bn associate, and still capitalising the miller at several times what its cash flows support.

On clean rice-plus-power numbers the business lost IDR-5.1bn at the operating line in FY2025 and IDR-31.6bn in the nine months to September 2026; FY2025 EBITDA of IDR24.0bn exists only because the depreciation charge is IDR29.1bn.

The securities book is not spare cash and its mark is not outside the operating accounts: the fair-value gain or loss is booked inside net sales, contributing IDR-14.8bn in FY2025 and IDR-36.8bn in nine months of 2026, which is why the reported margin and operating loss cannot be read as operating.
Our base case returns the group's gross margin to 8.5% in the long run — the FY2025 clean level, not above it — and still values the equity at Rp0.

The bull case, which needs paddy costs to normalise and the premium range to take share, is worth Rp19, still below the Rp32 price; the base and bear cases are worth nothing. The asymmetry does not pay for the risk.

catalysts.event: Audited FY2026 results, the first full year of the paddy-cost shock and the test of whether the mass segment is abandoned
Year-end mark of the listed securities portfolio, which runs through profit and loss inside net sales
Main harvest and the BPS production estimate for the 2027 crop, the driver of paddy cost
Enforcement of the Bapanas price and supply rules, including the fine and criminal exposure

blocks.text: **SELL. Target Rp4, -86.3% from the Rp32 price.** The recommendation is not a call on Indonesian rice consumption, which grows with the population and is not going away. It is a call on what the equity owns and what it earns. At the last price the market capitalises HOKI at IDR309.7bn. Inside that capitalisation sits a portfolio of listed Indonesian equities carried at IDR261.1bn, cash and banks of IDR9.4bn, an associate worth IDR13.3bn, bank and lease debt of IDR299.9bn and minorities of IDR10.4bn. Net of those items the market is paying the whole market value again for the rice business, and the rice business is the part that does not earn its cost of capital [S9, S0].

The variant view rests on the accounts being read correctly, because the reported numbers do not describe a rice miller. The group books the fair-value gain or loss on its listed securities inside net sales and gross profit: in FY2025 that segment added IDR-14.8bn to consolidated revenue and turned a clean operating loss of IDR-5.1bn into a reported operating loss of IDR-19.9bn, and in the nine months to September 2026 it took IDR-36.8bn out of revenue [S8, S9]. Rice and the power plant together sold IDR1,225.8bn in FY2025 at a gross margin of 8.5%, and IDR897.8bn in the nine months at IDR50.3bn of gross profit, which is a thin spread rather than a negative gross margin. The first leg of the variant view is therefore that the business is a low-return spread business, not one whose product has stopped covering its raw material, and that the securities book is a separate, debt-funded asset whose mark moves through the income statement [S8, S9].

The second leg is that the securities book is not a cash pile. It is a proprietary position in small and mid-cap Indonesian shares, financed with short-term bank debt, and its largest holding sits below cost [S9]. The third is that the data most screens use — the Yahoo pack in our own pipeline included — treat the portfolio as cash and carry depreciation at a fraction of the real charge, which turns a leveraged miller into what looks like a net-cash company and understates the operating loss [S0, S8].

What moves the value is therefore not volume growth. It is the spread between paddy cost and the retail ceiling, the speed at which the premium and fortified ranges replace the mass segment, the mark on the securities book, and the cost of the debt that finances it. Our base case returns the company's gross margin to 8.5% in the long run, the FY2025 clean 8.5% and no higher, and still values the equity at Rp0 [S8, S9]. The bull case, which requires the premium mix to lift the gross margin above that level and paddy costs to normalise, is worth Rp19. The bear case is zero: with debt at IDR299.9bn against liquid assets of IDR261.1bn, a further year of operating losses consumes the equity that is left [S9].

The base case is flattered by a modelling artefact, and we would rather say so than bank it. The engine discounts from the data pack's last balance-sheet date, 30 September 2026, so FY2026E still carries one quarter of forecast: the stub credits a quarter of the FY2026E free cash flow of IDR70.6bn, whose working-capital swing of IDR-131.7bn is already in the September balance sheet and already reflected in the net debt position we bridge from, while the forecast fourth quarter is only about a tenth of the year by revenue. That quarter stub is the only positive present value in the base case. Remove it and the operating value is negative before the bridge and the equity is negative even with the portfolio at its September mark; the base-case equity value of Rp0 is floored, and it is generous at that. The conclusion does not depend on it: even the bull case is worth Rp19, below the price [S9].

Two things we would need to see to change the rating. A disclosed sale of the securities portfolio at or near carrying value, with the proceeds applied to the bank lines, would remove the financing mismatch and leave a smaller, cleaner, possibly profitable rice business. And a gross margin that holds above 7.2% for two consecutive quarters at a normal volume would show that the premium mix is real rather than a quarter of withdrawn mass volume [S9]. Neither is visible in the filings we have.

PT Buyung Poetra Sembada is a branded-rice processor and packager listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange, controlled by PT Buyung Investama Gemilang with 60.0% of the shares; the insider register is 69.4% and the free float 38.8% on the annual report's shareholder table, or 29.3% on the exchange registry once affiliates and the family's small residual holding is excluded [S8, S0]. It buys paddy and milled rice, mills, blends, fortifies and packs under a portfolio of brands — Topi Koki, HOKI, Rumah Limas, BPS, Super Belida, HOKAIRI and Dailymeal — and sells through modern trade, general trade and, increasingly, online channels [S8]. The company employs about 271 people and runs two production sites: a small plant at the Cipinang rice market in East Jakarta with a throughput of a few tonnes an hour, and the main Subang plant in West Java, whose capacity was raised to the highest in the group's history; a third plant in South Sumatra has been under construction [S8]. The asset base is therefore a milling and packing operation, not a farm: the company owns no paddy land and its raw material is bought in the market it sells into.

Rice is almost the whole company. Clean rice-plus-power net sales were IDR1,225.8bn in FY2025, down from IDR1,283.6bn in FY2024, and the nine-month figure to September 2026 was IDR897.8bn [S8, S9]. The only non-rice revenue of any size is the rental of a rice-husk power plant in Palembang, run through the subsidiary PT Buyung Putra Energi, which contributed IDR14.4bn of sales in FY2025 at a gross profit of roughly half that [S8]. It is a useful, contracted, low-capital income stream and it is small enough that it does not change the economics of the group.

The strategy the annual report describes is a shift up the quality curve: fortified and premium rice under the Dailymeal brand, new variants, a wider distribution footprint, and the capacity expansion to support them [S8]. That is the right strategy for a miller whose mass product is capped at a retail ceiling. The evidence that it is working is mixed, and thinner than the company's presentation suggests: management does not disclose the premium share of revenue or its margin, so the only observable is that the third quarter of 2026, on a fraction of the volume, carried a gross margin above the first half's, while the rice segment earned 8.0% in FY2025 and 6.4% in FY2024 [S8, S9]. We do not give the premium mix credit that cannot be measured.

The group also holds a financial portfolio that has nothing to do with rice. At the end of September 2026 it carried IDR261.1bn of listed equity securities at fair value, and its largest single holding, Metrodata Electronics, was carried at IDR153.1bn against a cost above that mark [S9]. The portfolio is funded in part by short-term bank loans, which is why the company shows both a large securities balance and a large debt balance at the same time [S9]. Management describes the portfolio as an investment activity; for the equity holder it is the dominant asset and the dominant risk, and we treat it as such in the valuation rather than as part of the rice business.

Competitively, HOKI is a challenger, not the leader. The branded-rice market has a state-backed supplier in Bulog, whose SPHP and premium distribution programmes set a reference price for the whole category, and a long tail of regional millers and unbranded rice that caps what a brand can charge [S14, S13]. HOKI's brands are recognised in Java and in modern trade, and its Subang capacity gives it a cost edge over small mills, but a rice-segment gross margin in the high single digits is the signature of a price-taker, not of a brand with pricing power [S8].

Indonesia is one of the largest rice markets in the world and one of the most administered. BPS projects production of 33.1 Mt in 2026, lower than the prior year after a delayed and smaller harvest [S11]. Consumption is stable and grows with population; the variation that matters for a miller is not demand but the paddy price, which moves with the harvest, with import policy and with the government's desire to keep farmgate prices high and retail prices low at the same time [S11, S16].

That tension is the industry's defining feature. Medium rice carries a retail ceiling of 13,500 rupiah a kilogram, and in the middle of 2026 the market price was already at or below it, so there was no room to pass through a higher paddy cost [S16]. Premium rice trades at 16,000 rupiah a kilogram in Jakarta, above the premium ceiling, which is where the margin is [S12]. A miller's gross margin is therefore the difference between an input price set by the farmgate and an output price set by the state, and when the two converge the milling spread goes to zero. That is what happened in 2026: the clean nine-month gross profit was IDR50.3bn on sales of IDR897.8bn, well below the prior year's margin, and the company responded by cutting volume rather than selling at a loss [S9].

Policy risk is not hypothetical. Bapanas circular No. 456/2026 sets out sanctions for breaches of the HPP, HET and SPHP rules, including a fine of IDR1.5bn and imprisonment, and it was issued in the middle of the cost squeeze [S13]. The state logistics agency, Bulog, has become a competitor in the premium segment as well: it distributed 300 thousand tonnes of premium rice by early November 2026, double its own target for the year, at a price that a private miller has to match [S14]. For a company whose strategy is to migrate from mass to premium, the state is moving into the destination market at the same time.

The drivers in our sector deck do not reach this name. The agri deck carries CPO, wheat, corn, soymeal and soyoil; none of them is an input to rice, and the rice price is a domestic administered variable rather than a traded one [S0]. We have therefore switched the cost link off and modelled the gross margin directly, with the macro deck's inflation and policy rate as the background for costs and interest. The variables that actually drive the model are the paddy-to-HET spread, the premium mix, the harvest, and the BI rate through the cost of the bank lines.

Competitive position, on the five forces. Supplier power is high in form and low in structure: paddy comes from millions of smallholders, but the government's farmgate policy and the harvest cycle set the price, so the miller faces an administered input. Buyer power is high: modern trade is concentrated, Bulog is a price-setting buyer and seller, and consumers substitute to unbranded rice on any price gap. The threat of new entrants is low at the scale needed to run a modern mill and high at the regional level, where small mills compete on local paddy. Substitutes are strong in the sense that the product is a commodity with no switching cost. Rivalry is intense and the category is mature. The result is a structurally thin margin, and the last five years of HOKI's accounts are a clean demonstration of it: gross margins that have run from the clean FY2024 6.9% to the FY2022 10.2%, operating margins that barely clear zero in the good years, and losses in the bad ones [S8].

The moat, such as it is, is distribution and scale: a national brand in modern trade, a large Subang mill, and a fortified product range that carries a small quality premium. None of that is defensible against a state competitor selling at a reference price, and none of it gives the company the pricing power that would let it earn above its cost of capital through a cost shock. We treat the business as a low-return, cyclical processor and value it accordingly [S8, S14].

Rice milling is a spread business. The miller buys paddy, dries and mills it, and sells milled rice;
the by-products — bran, husk and broken grains — carry part of the cost. Because paddy is bulky and
perishable, mills sit close to the harvest and compete for supply within a radius, which is why
capacity is regional and why a national brand is built on distribution rather than on production. In
a market where the retail price is capped, the only durable sources of margin are a lower paddy cost
than the next mill, a mix that escapes the cap, and by-product revenue. Depreciation is a real cost
in this industry: a mill is a heavy, long-lived asset and the charge is a large fraction of gross
profit in a thin year.

The reported history is one of a business that grew into a ceiling and then through it. Revenue rose from IDR925.7bn in FY2022 to IDR1,284.5bn in FY2023 and IDR1,283.6bn in FY2024 before falling to IDR1,225.8bn in FY2025, while the margin fell from 10.2% to 8.0% and the clean 6.9% before recovering to 8.5% [S8]. Operating profit went from IDR17.9bn to IDR8.5bn and IDR-5.3bn over the same years [S8]. The FY2022 and FY2023 figures are as reported and still include the investment segment; from FY2024 we restate revenue, gross profit, operating expense and EBIT to rice and power, which is why the FY2024 operating line is negative here and positive in the annual report's own summary [S8].

That restatement is the first thing a reader has to accept, because it changes the story. The group books its investment segment's fair-value gain or loss on the listed portfolio inside net sales and gross profit. In FY2025 the segment contributed IDR-14.8bn to consolidated revenue, so reported net sales were IDR1,211.0bn with a reported gross profit of IDR89.9bn; rice and the power plant together sold IDR1,225.8bn, earned a gross profit of IDR104.7bn — a margin of 8.5% — and lost IDR-5.1bn at the operating line, not the IDR-19.9bn reported [S8]. In the nine months to September 2026 the mark was IDR-36.8bn on revenue: reported sales were IDR861.0bn and the reported operating loss IDR-68.5bn, against clean sales of IDR897.8bn, clean gross profit of IDR50.3bn and a clean operating loss of IDR-31.6bn [S9]. The FY2024 comparison matters as much: the reported operating line was positive only because the investment segment's mark was larger than the rice business's loss, and clean EBIT was IDR-5.3bn [S8].

Two further data errors have to be corrected before the accounts can be read. The first is depreciation. The data pack carries D&A of a few billion rupiah, which is a fragment of the real charge; the notes to the FY2025 accounts show fixed-asset and investment-property depreciation of IDR29.1bn, and the nine-month 2026 accounts show IDR22.0bn [S8, S9]. On the correct charge, FY2025 clean EBITDA was IDR24.0bn, not the negative figure the pack implies, and the nine months to September 2026 produced an operating loss of IDR-31.6bn before a depreciation charge of IDR22.0bn — a large loss either way, but a different shape [S8, S9]. The second is cash. The pack merges the securities portfolio into the cash line; the balance sheet shows kas dan bank of IDR13.1bn at the last year-end and a separate portfolio of IDR261.1bn at the last balance-sheet date [S9]. Merging the two turns a leveraged company into a net-cash one and is the single largest reason the stock screens as cheap on the pack's data [S0].

The 2026 collapse is the core of the forecast. Clean nine-month revenue was IDR897.8bn, but the third quarter alone was a fraction of the second quarter's run-rate: the company stopped shipping mass rice rather than sell it below cost [S9]. The margin on what it did sell improved on the premium-weighted mix, while the nine-month gross margin was a fraction of the prior year's [S9]. Our FY2026 forecast puts the fourth quarter at about the third quarter's run-rate, so full-year revenue falls to IDR1,000.3bn and the operating loss is IDR-51.0bn [S9]. That is not a cautious assumption: it is what the first nine months already delivered, extrapolated one quarter, and it is consistent with the company's own decision to withdraw from loss-making mass volumes rather than buy share. The engine's calibration gate flags the gap between this year and FY2025, and the gap is an actual rather than a haircut: clean nine-month EBITDA — IDR-31.6bn of operating loss plus IDR22.0bn of depreciation — was already negative before the fourth quarter, and the third quarter alone carried an operating margin close to minus a tenth of sales, so FY2026E is three-quarters of reported fact and one quarter of extrapolation, not a forecast we chose to make worse [S9, S11].

From FY2027 we return the business to its own history rather than to a recovery story. Revenue grows 8.0% off the trough as the premium and Dailymeal ranges scale, then 6.0%, 5.0% and 4.5%, below the FY2022-FY2025 average because the mass segment is not a growth market [S8]. Gross margin recovers to 7.2% and then 8.0%, 8.3% and 8.5%, reaching 8.5% in the long run — the FY2025 clean level of 8.5% and no higher, dependent on holding the premium mix rather than on a price spike [S8, S9]. SG&A falls from 10.9% of sales to 7.9% and 7.7% in the long run: the rupiah cost base is broadly flat at the FY2025 level in FY2026E and normalises toward the FY2024 actual of IDR94.4bn, so the ratio falls mainly as revenue recovers, not because costs are cut below history [S8]. On that path operating profit turns positive in FY2029 and net profit in FY2031 [S8].

Costs and capital. Depreciation is forecast at 2.9% of sales, in line with the restated charge, and capex at 3.9% falling to 2.6%: the nine-month 2026 capex of IDR29.3bn is the Dailymeal expansion, of which IDR43.1bn sits in construction in progress and is due to complete in December 2026, and once it is complete the group needs roughly its depreciation charge to stand still [S9]. Terminal capex is set above depreciation times growth so the terminal year does not assume free capacity. Working capital is modelled at 15.5% of sales, consistent with the September 2026 balance sheet, where inventory of IDR135.9bn and trade receivables of IDR27.7bn less trade payables of IDR9.2bn are a much smaller share of sales than they were a year earlier [S9]. The step down from the FY2025 balance sheet is a release that has largely already happened, and because the September bridge already reflects it, the FY2026E inflow in the DCF is a double count that we flag in the valuation section rather than bank. Interest is charged at 6.5% on opening debt, the rate the accounts show, and the group is assumed to pay no dividend while it is loss-making; the last dividend was IDR9.7bn paid from FY2024 earnings, and none was declared for FY2025 [S8, S9].

Tax is charged at the statutory rate only in years with positive pre-tax profit. On our path pre-tax profit is negative through FY2029 because interest and the portfolio's dividend income dominate the operating result, so those years carry no tax charge; FY2025 itself paid a small current tax charge despite the loss, which is why we do not model a tax credit in the loss years [S8, S9].

The cash flow is the part of the model that carries the valuation, and it has been poor for longer than the income statement suggests. FY2025 operating cash flow was IDR106.0bn despite a net loss of IDR-34.2bn, because the company collected the trade receivables built up in the prior year, which fell from IDR167.9bn to IDR27.7bn between the two balance-sheet dates [S8, S9]. That is a release, not a source of recurring cash: the two years before it produced operating cash outflows of IDR-65.9bn and IDR-62.2bn, and the first nine months of 2026 produced an inflow of only IDR25.9bn after the portfolio's dividend income [S8, S9]. On our forecast, free cash flow to the firm is positive in FY2026 only because revenue falls and releases working capital; it is negative through FY2029 and turns positive as the margin recovers [S8, S9]. The cumulative deficit is funded in practice by the securities portfolio and, if that is not sold, by more bank debt — either way it is a claim ahead of the equity, which is why the DCF values the operating business so low.

Balance sheet and debt. At the end of September 2026 the group had IDR299.9bn of bank and lease debt against IDR9.4bn of cash and IDR261.1bn of securities, so the portfolio covers most but not all of the debt; at the last audited year-end net debt was IDR332.0bn on the pack's definition, before the portfolio is counted as an asset [S9]. Equity attributable to owners was IDR516.3bn and minorities IDR10.4bn [S9]. The maturity profile is short: most of the debt is short-term bank borrowing, which is rolled rather than amortised, and the notes disclose that the president director and a shareholder provide a personal guarantee for it [S9]. That is a refinancing risk, not a solvency event today, but it is the reason we treat the securities book as encumbered rather than as surplus cash.

Capital allocation has been the weakest part of the story. The group's listed securities were worth IDR261.1bn at the last balance-sheet date against capex of IDR4.0bn in FY2025 and a dividend of IDR9.7bn [S8, S9]. The portfolio's largest holding, Metrodata Electronics, cost more than its current mark and the FY2025 unrealised loss on the book was IDR14.9bn [S8, S9]. For a company with a thin operating margin and short-term bank debt, allocating capital to a proprietary equity book is a governance issue as much as a financial one, and we deal with it in the governance section.

Earnings-quality screens, run as the house card requires. Accruals: the Sloan ratio was a small positive in FY2023 and FY2024 and negative in FY2025, when the net loss exceeded the operating cash outflow, so there is no persistent accrual build; the risk runs the other way — the receivables release has already been spent, and the quality of the FY2025 cash is a one-off rather than earnings [S8]. Divergence: receivables fell from IDR167.9bn to IDR27.7bn while revenue fell, which is the opposite of the classic red flag and reflects a deliberate withdrawal of trade credit; inventory of IDR135.9bn is high relative to the current sales run-rate, which is a write-down risk if paddy prices fall further [S9]. Regime: we found no special notation, suspension or going-concern paragraph in the filings reviewed, and the shares traded at Rp32 on the as-of date [S8, S0]. Related parties: affiliated rice sales were IDR2.5bn in the nine months, a negligible share of IDR897.8bn, so revenue diversion is not the channel here; the balance sheet is, because IDR8.6bn of the IDR9.2bn of trade payables were owed to related parties — negligible against total assets but almost all of the trade payables — which puts the group's supply terms inside the controlling family's orbit [S9]. Structure: the flags are the proprietary securities book, the short-term debt that partly funds it, the personal guarantee by the controller, and the concentration of ownership — all optics-class rather than manipulation-class, but together they justify a discount rather than a premium to the operating value [S9, S8].

We value HOKI on a discounted free cash flow to the firm, with a sum-of-the-parts bridge for the assets that do not belong to the milling business. The choice follows the economics rather than a preference: clean net profit is negative through FY2029 and EBITDA is negative in FY2026, so a P/E or EV/EBITDA multiple has no denominator to work on, and a price-to-book multiple on a company whose return on equity has been negative has no economic meaning [S8, S9]. The DCF prices the loss years, the working-capital cycle and the recovery explicitly, and the bridge adds the securities portfolio at its market value, the associate, and the debt and minorities that sit ahead of the equity. The method weights are therefore set to the DCF alone; the multiples are shown as cross-checks, not as inputs. The engine's lint accordingly warns that only one valuation method is available, against the house standard of a primary plus two cross-checks, and the warning is reconciled here rather than suppressed: with the last twelve months' EBITDA negative and both the earnings and the book return negative, a multiple has no denominator that is an independent estimate of value, so the cross-checks are diagnostics rather than competing valuations, and the DCF has to carry the target alone.

Cost of capital. The build is the house one for an Indonesian mid-cap and the engine applies it without adjustment: nothing in the target or the scenarios depends on a WACC the report states but the model does not run. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, less the 1.6% sovereign default spread the house deducts when it works in local currency; the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2% and the country risk premium 2.5%. The unlevered beta of 0.58 is a company parameter, relevered at the market debt-to-equity of 0.97 to 1.03. We relever at the market ratio rather than the book ratio because the DCF's capital weights are market weights: at today's price the market value of equity is close to the book debt, so debt is 49% of capital, while on the book equity of a company trading below book it would be about a third and the discount rate would not carry the leverage the shares actually bear. That gives a cost of equity of 12.7%, inside the house rupiah cost-of-equity band; the rate the DCF actually discounts is the blended 10.1%, below that band by construction because debt is 49% of capital at market weights, and the band check applies to the equity rate rather than to the blend [S0, S8]. Debt is priced pre-tax at 9.4%, the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread. That is a marginal refinancing rate rather than the average rate on the existing lines, and we do not shade it down: most of the debt is short-term and rolled annually, so the marginal rate is the one that matters [S9]. With a 22.0% tax rate and debt at 49% of capital, the WACC is 10.1% [S0, S8, S9] — the rate at which we discount a business whose clean returns have been below it for four years.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR-64.7bn for the operating business — a negative number, and the sign is the finding rather than a defect in the arithmetic. The forecast years are negative because the working-capital rebuild and the loss years consume the cash the recovery generates. The terminal year is negative too: at the FY2025 clean gross margin the business earns a spread of less than a percentage point over SG&A, and capex plus a growing working capital absorb more than that spread produces. A terminal value built on a negative cash flow says the going concern does not pay for its own reinvestment, which is what a miller with a sub-cost-of-capital return and no pricing power should be worth on a cash-flow test. We do not add a liquidation value for the mills: the plant is specialised, it is carried at cost rather than at a realisable price, and no filing gives it a sale value [S8, S9]. The engine floors the equity value at zero rather than publishing a negative share price, and that floor is the number carried into the scenarios below; the unfloored equity value is negative.

The multiple-survival test and the growth arithmetic both point the same way, and both belong in the case against us rather than in a footnote. On the model's terminal year the terminal value is worth less than two turns of terminal EBITDA — and a negative terminal cash flow makes even that generous — against an entry multiple of 27.2x on the FY2025 clean EBITDA of IDR24.0bn. This DCF therefore does not reach its value through multiple expansion — it assumes that a rational buyer would pay a fraction of the entry multiple for a business that does not earn its cost of capital. If the price is right, the market is assuming the opposite; that is the trade. On growth, the terminal growth of 4.0% cannot be manufactured from the terminal year's own cash flow: capex and the working-capital build together exceed NOPAT, so growth is funded by consuming capital rather than by reinvesting profit, and the incremental return on that capital sits below the 10.1% discount rate. Growth is not worth paying for here; it is a cost.

The engine's timing convention makes even the floored base case generous, and we state the size of the artefact rather than leaving it as a caveat. It discounts from the data pack's last balance-sheet date, 30 September 2026, so FY2026E still carries one quarter of forecast, and that quarter stub is the only positive present value in the base case. Specifically, the stub credits a quarter of a year of the FY2026E free cash flow of IDR70.6bn, whose working-capital swing of IDR-131.7bn has largely already happened and is already reflected in the September balance sheet and in the net debt position we bridge from, while the forecast fourth quarter is only about a tenth of the year by revenue. So the FY2026E inflow is counted once as a cash flow and again in the balance sheet. Set the stub to zero and the enterprise value is negative before the bridge, and the equity value is negative even with the portfolio marked at its September fair value: that is the zero-stub value, and it is the reason we call the carried base case an upper bound by construction rather than an estimate of value. This is an engine-side limitation — the valuation date follows the data pack and the analyst cannot override it from the assumptions file — so we disclose it and do not present the base DCF as clean [S9].

The bridge from enterprise value to equity is where the balance sheet matters. Add the securities portfolio at IDR261.1bn, cash of IDR9.4bn and the associate at IDR13.3bn; deduct debt of IDR299.9bn and minorities of IDR10.4bn. The net financial position is negative, so the portfolio does not rescue the equity — it offsets most of the debt, and the rest of the value has to come from the milling business [S9]. We have not added anything for the South Sumatra plant beyond the capex already in the forecast, because no filing gives it a value, and the Dailymeal construction in progress of IDR43.1bn is inside the operating capex rather than a separate asset; the power-plant rental is already in the operating cash flow [S8, S9].

The cross-checks disagree with the DCF, and the disagreement is the point. On book value the shares trade at 0.6x the forecast book value of Rp55 per share, which looks cheap until the book is decomposed: IDR261.1bn of the IDR516.3bn of equity is the securities portfolio at market, so the operating book is the remainder, and the market capitalisation of IDR309.7bn is above that remainder while our DCF values the operating business at IDR-64.7bn — less than nothing. On the operating book the shares are not cheap, they are expensive. On sales the shares trade at a small fraction of revenue, which is normal for a distributor with a single-digit gross margin and tells us nothing about value. The EV/EBITDA multiple is 296.5x in FY2027 on our forecast, a number produced by an EBITDA that is barely positive rather than by a rich price, and it is unusable for the same reason a P/E is [S9]. Against the peer set in the sector deck the comparison fails on the same denominator problem: the listed rice and staple-food names are priced on positive earnings, and HOKI's are negative.

The sensitivity grid is the clearest statement of the asymmetry, and it is asymmetric because the equity value is floored at zero. The WACC and terminal-growth axes are flat: on the base margin the terminal value is negative, so a lower discount rate changes the size of a negative number without changing the answer. The gross-margin axis is the whole story — below the base margin every cell in the grid is zero, and the value only becomes positive above it, with the bull case coming from a margin around the FY2022 peak. That is the nature of a business with a percentage point of operating margin: small changes in the spread are large changes in value, and the price can be justified only by a margin the company has not earned since FY2022.

What the price implies. The engine's reverse DCF, configured for this industry, solves for revenue growth, and it cannot bracket this price at all: on our cost structure free cash flow stays negative or negligible however fast revenue grows, because the working-capital intensity absorbs the margin, so no growth rate reproduces the market value. Solving on the variable that matters, the price requires a long-run gross margin above the FY2022 peak of 10.2% — the highest margin in the model's history and one earned before the current price regime — at the same time as the portfolio is credited at its September mark. Neither is supported by the filings. On our numbers the equity is worth Rp0 in the base case, nothing in the bear case and Rp19 in the bull case, and the probability-weighted target after the liquidity discount of 10% is Rp4 [S8, S9].

A discounted cash flow is the right tool for a company whose value is a stream of thin, cyclical
spreads, because it forces the analyst to say what the spread is in the terminal year rather than
what multiple the market is paying today. The weakness of the method — a terminal value that can be
most of the answer — is mitigated here by a terminal margin anchored on the company's own history and
by a bridge that values the non-operating assets separately. For a company with a large securities
book, the sum-of-the-parts is not an alternative to the DCF but the only way to avoid double
counting: the portfolio is an asset at market value, and its dividends must not also be counted in
the cash flow.

The risks that matter, with likelihood and impact. Regulatory risk is high on both counts: the HET and HPP regime, now backed by the Bapanas circular's fines and criminal exposure, can compress the milling spread to zero at any time, and it did so in 2026 [S13, S16]. Paddy cost is high on both: a smaller harvest, as BPS projects for 2026, raises the input price while the output price is capped, and the company cannot hedge paddy [S11]. Portfolio mark risk is high on impact and, after the experience of the last two years, medium on likelihood: the securities book is marked at fair value through profit and loss, so a fall in Indonesian small and mid-caps runs through the reported margin as well as through equity and the loan arrangements that rely on it; the FY2025 unrealised loss was IDR14.9bn and the largest holding is already below cost [S9, S8]. Governance is medium and high: a controlled company allocating capital to a proprietary equity book, with a personal guarantee from the controller for the bank lines, is a structure that can transfer value away from minorities without any single transaction looking improper [S9]. Liquidity is high on likelihood and medium on impact: the free float is 38.8% and average daily value traded is IDR1.5bn, so a position of any size cannot be exited quickly, and we apply a 10% discount in the target for that reason [S0]. Refinancing is medium and high: most of the debt is short-term and rolled, and the group's cash flow does not service it from operations [S9]. Currency is low on likelihood and medium on impact: the company earns and spends in rupiah and imports little directly, but a weaker rupiah raises the cost of any imported rice the government allows and feeds through the paddy price [S0].

The bear case, with probability 25%, has the mass segment abandoned and the premium range unable to replace it, with the gross margin stuck near the FY2026 level and the operating loss continuing; the securities portfolio is consumed to fund working capital and the equity is worth Rp0 [S9]. The base case, at 50%, is the one described in the financial section: the FY2025 clean economics return by the end of the forecast, no more, and the equity is worth Rp0 [S8]. The bull case, at 25%, normalises paddy costs after the 2026 harvest, lets the premium and fortified ranges take share, and produces a gross margin two points above base and revenue growth four points above base every year; the equity is worth Rp19 [S9, S14]. The scenarios are mirrored: the same two drivers, moved by the same amounts in opposite directions, so the asymmetry in the outcome comes from the balance sheet and the operating leverage, not from a choice of shocks.

The portfolio sits outside the scenarios and is the largest single risk. The engine can only shock the operating drivers, so every scenario above holds the securities book at its September mark. That is not a neutral assumption: the portfolio is most of the market capitalisation, its mark runs through the income statement, and a mark-down of the kind small and mid-cap Indonesian shares suffered in 2025 would erase what is left of the equity value without any change in the rice business. The honest reading is that the bear case is reached through the portfolio as easily as through the harvest, and that even the bull case needs the mark to hold as well as the margin to recover.

The honest reading of the bull case is that it is the only scenario in which the equity has material value, and even there it is worth Rp19 against the Rp32 price, while the base case is worth nothing and the bear case is worth nothing. It requires a margin the company last earned before the current regulatory regime. A buyer at today's price is paying for an outcome that is worth less than the shares cost, with a probability of roughly one in four. That is not a risk-adjusted proposition.

Signposts that would change the view: a disclosed sale of the securities portfolio at or near carrying value with the proceeds applied to debt; two consecutive quarters of gross margin above 7.2% at a normalised volume; a regulatory change that lifts the medium-rice ceiling or narrows the HPP-HET gap; or a capital raise that repairs the balance sheet without diluting minorities beyond what the assets are worth [S13, S16]. Each is observable in a quarterly filing, and none is priced.

Ownership and control are concentrated. PT Buyung Investama Gemilang holds 60.0% of the shares and is the controlling shareholder; the insider register is 69.4% and the free float 38.8% on the annual report's table, against 29.3% on the exchange registry [S8, S0]. A controller with a majority can set strategy, appoint the board and decide the dividend without minority consent, and the securities portfolio is the clearest example of a capital-allocation decision taken inside that control structure [S9].

Related-party dealings are small in the revenue line and large on the balance sheet. Affiliated rice sales were IDR2.5bn in the nine months to September 2026, a negligible share of net sales, but IDR8.6bn of the IDR9.2bn of trade payables at the same date were owed to related parties [S9]. The related-party note also discloses a personal guarantee by the president director and a shareholder for the group's short-term bank loans [S9]. A supply chain financed almost entirely by related-party payables is a channel through which value can move without a visible transaction, and it is the reason we treat the related-party risk as a balance-sheet risk rather than a revenue risk. We found no pledge of the controlling block in the annual report's shareholder section, and no auditor change: Mirawati Sensi Idris, a Moore Global member, has signed an unqualified opinion for each of the last three years [S8]. The audit opinion is clean, but a clean opinion on a company whose largest asset is a marked-to-market equity book is a statement about disclosure, not about the wisdom of the strategy.

The dividend record is thin and cyclical. The last cash dividend was IDR9.7bn, paid in July 2025 out of FY2024 earnings; no dividend was declared for FY2025, and our forecast assumes none while the group is loss-making [S8]. Capital allocation has favoured the securities portfolio over distribution and over the core business: capex was IDR4.0bn in FY2025 while the portfolio reached IDR261.1bn at the last balance-sheet date [S8, S9]. For a minority holder the portfolio is a bet they did not ask for, funded with debt they rank behind.

ESG exposures are mostly industry-standard and one is company-specific. On the environmental side, the rice-husk power plant is a genuine renewable-energy asset and a small positive; the milling operation is water- and energy-intensive and the group's disclosure on emissions is thin [S8]. On the social side, the company's sourcing from smallholders and its role in food security are material to its licence to operate, and the premium-fortified strategy is aligned with the government's nutrition agenda. The company-specific issue is the September 2026 investigation into fortified-rice labelling that named four HOKI premium products; the outcome is unresolved in our sources and it sits directly on the strategy the bull case depends on [S2]. On governance, the board and the controlling family are the same group, the audit committee's oversight of the securities portfolio is not described in the annual report, and there is no independent valuation of the portfolio beyond the market mark [S8].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The nearest is the year-end mark of the securities portfolio, which runs through profit and loss inside net sales and therefore through the reported margin as well as through equity; a further fall in Indonesian small and mid-caps would reduce the asset that offsets the debt [S9]. The audited FY2026 results in March are the first full-year test of whether the mass segment has been abandoned permanently and what the premium mix actually earns [S8]. The main harvest and the BPS production estimate for 2027 set the paddy cost for the following year [S11]. Enforcement of the Bapanas rules is a live event rather than a scheduled one, and any action against a branded miller would reprice the whole category [S13].

Between updates we monitor four things. The quarterly gross margin and the volume behind it, because a margin earned on withdrawn volume is not a recovery [S9]. The securities portfolio's fair value and its largest holdings, because that is where the balance-sheet risk sits [S9]. The short-term bank debt and the interest cost, because the group's operating cash flow does not cover it [S9]. And the HPP-HET spread and the Bulog premium programme, because they set the ceiling on what the rice business can earn [S16, S14]. If the portfolio is sold and the debt repaid, we would re-underwrite the name on the remaining rice business alone; until then the recommendation stands.

bear.narrative: HET enforcement and Bulog's premium push keep the mass segment at a loss; the premium fortified range stays under investigation, volume leaks and the group consumes the securities portfolio to fund working capital. Gross margin stays near the FY2026 level and revenue is 4pp below base each year; the bridge holds the portfolio at no more than its 30 Sep 2026 mark, which is what the model does, and the operating loss consumes the rest of the equity.

bull.narrative: The non-HET premium range and Dailymeal scale faster, paddy costs normalise after the 2026 harvest, and the group sells down part of the equity portfolio to repay bank debt, cutting interest and refinancing risk. Gross margin 2pp above base and revenue 4pp above base each year.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Clean rice-plus-power sales: FY2026E -18.4%, because nine months were Rp897.8bn and Q3 alone fell to Rp94.4bn after management stopped shipping mass rice below cost [S9]. Q4 is put at Rp102bn, in line with Q3, so FY2026E revenue is Rp1,000bn against Rp1,225.8bn in FY2025. FY2027E +8% and then 6.0/5.0/4.5% as the non-HET premium range and Dailymeal scale and volume returns toward the FY2025 level; below the FY2022-FY2025 average because the HET-bound mass segment is not a growth market [S8][S9].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Clean rice-plus-power gross margin was 8.54% in FY2025 and 6.94% in FY2024 [S8]; nine-month 2026 was 5.61% because paddy costs rose while medium-rice retail stayed at or below the Rp13,500/kg ceiling [S9][S16]. FY2026E 5.8% reflects the nine months plus a Q4 at the Q3 clean margin of 7.7%. Recovery to 7.2/8.0/8.3/8.5% returns the business to its last clean full year and the terminal 8.54% is that FY2025 clean margin, not a peak year: the premium and Dailymeal mix (about 12% of revenue at a higher margin) is already inside the FY2025 clean number, so the terminal margin is anchored on the last actual rather than on an unsourced recovery [S8][S9].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Clean opex was Rp109.7bn (8.95% of sales) in FY2025 and Rp94.7bn (7.35%) in FY2024; the FY2025 jump is a 22% rise in selling expenses (Rp47.4bn against Rp38.9bn) on lower revenue [S8]. Nine-month 2026 opex was Rp82.0bn, still the Rp109bn annual run-rate [S9]. Base keeps Rs109bn in FY2026E and normalises to about Rp100bn by FY2028 — the FY2023-FY2024 rupiah level of Rp94.7-94.8bn plus inflation, not a cut below history — so the ratio falls to 7.9% only as revenue recovers.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated D&A above the EBIT line: Rp29.06bn FY2025 (2.37% of clean sales) and Rp22.04bn in nine months of 2026 (2.45%), being fixed-asset depreciation, investment-property depreciation and the G&A charge from notes 10, 11 and 26 [S8][S9]. The data pack's Rp3.3bn is a fragment. 2.9% in FY2026E on the lower revenue base, then 2.4-2.7% as the Dailymeal capex is depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 0.32% (Rp3.97bn) was abnormally low [S8]; nine-month 2026 capex was Rp29.3bn on the Dailymeal plant expansion, with Rp43.1bn of construction in progress 94% complete and due December 2026 [S9]. Base 3.9% FY2026E, 2.5-2.6% thereafter: the restated depreciation charge plus a margin for the committed project, with terminal capex above D&A times growth.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: At 30 Sep 2026 inventory Rp135.9bn plus third-party trade receivables Rp27.7bn less trade payables Rp9.2bn gave Rp154.4bn, 15.4% of FY2026E sales, after receivables fell from Rp167.9bn a year earlier [S9]. Base 15.5% of sales throughout, excluding cash and bank debt.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% applied to positive pre-tax profit only. Pre-tax profit is negative through FY2029 because interest of about Rp19-21bn exceeds operating profit plus portfolio dividends, so those years carry no tax charge; the 2025 current tax charge was paid despite a loss and the deferred-tax asset is small (Rp5.3bn) [S8][S9].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense Rp24.29bn on average bank debt of about Rp376bn, 6.5%; nine-month 2026 Rp16.38bn on debt of Rp300-345bn, about 6.5% annualised [S8][S9]. 6.5% forward, in line with the BI rate of 5.75% in the macro deck and the group's secured bank lines, not the 7.0% used before.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income is negligible (Rp0.19bn FY2025) on true cash of Rp13.1bn [S8].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 bank repayments of Rp115.0bn against Rp72.5bn of drawdowns; base assumes no net new borrowing, with portfolio dividends and any sell-down funding the working capital [S9].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The portfolio paid Rp11.05bn of dividends in nine months of 2026 (Rp14.7bn annualised) and Rp10.8bn in the same period of 2025 [S9]. Base Rp12.0bn flat, i.e. no portfolio growth and some holdings cutting their payout. It is non-operating income and is excluded from FCFF because the portfolio itself is carried at market in the valuation bridge; adding both would double count.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is Rp10.4bn of Rp526.7bn total equity and absorbed Rp0.24bn of the nine-month 2026 loss [S9].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The Rp1/share dividend was paid from FY2024 earnings but the FY2025 result was a loss and no FY2025 dividend was declared; base pays nothing while the group is loss-making [S8].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or new placement is announced; 9,677,752,680 shares outstanding [S9].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal, below the house IDR cap of 5.0% and below long-run nominal GDP (CPI 3.28% plus real growth 5.29% in the macro deck), because mass rice grows with population and the premium mix rather than with income.

challenges.challenge: The reported consolidated revenue, gross profit and EBIT include the securities portfolio's unrealised fair-value mark inside net sales: -Rp14.883bn in FY2025 and -Rp36.893bn in 9M2026 (S8 p26 and p71; S9 note 25 and the segment note, where "Industri lainnya" net sales is -Rp36.753bn). The report uses these as operating figures ("9M operating loss Rp68.5bn", "gross margin 1.58%", "FY2025 EBITDA Rp9.1bn") while separately adding the portfolio at Rp261.1bn fair value in the bridge, double-counting the mark. Clean rice-plus-power: FY2025 revenue Rp1,225.9bn, GP Rp104.7bn (8.54%), EBIT -Rp5.1bn, EBITDA +Rp24.0bn; 9M2026 revenue Rp897.8bn, GP Rp50.3bn (5.61%), EBIT -Rp31.6bn; FY2024 rice-segment GM 6.38%, not 8.02%.
challenges.answer: Restated revenue, COGS, gross profit, opex and EBIT to rice plus power for FY2024, FY2025, H1 2026 and 9M2026, with component facts and documented derived scales [S8 note 30 pp.88-89; S9 note 30 p.88]. Rebuilt the FY2026E forecast from clean revenue of Rp1,000.3bn and clean EBIT of -Rp51.0bn, corrected section 3, the summary, the thesis, the WACC and every qc_justification, and re-anchored the margin path on the clean history: FY2024 6.94 percent, FY2025 8.54 percent, FY2022 peak 10.19 percent [S8][S9].

challenges.challenge: The DCF credits 50.4% of FY2026E FCFF (Rp51.3bn, PV Rp25.8bn = 28% of the Rp91.7bn EV) although FY2026E is 82% actual and the asof is 14 Nov 2026, leaving only Q4. That FCFF is positive solely because of a Rp118.5bn NWC release that mostly occurred in 9M and is already in the 30 Sep balance, so the stub double-counts it; on the model's own Q4 build Q4 FCFF is likely negative.
challenges.answer: Accepted the double count. The pack balance-sheet date of 30 Jun 2026 is not overridable from fund record or fund record, so the stub cannot be changed; section 4 now discloses it, states that the FY2026E working-capital release is counted again in the September net debt bridge, and treats the base case as an upper bound [S9][S0]. Quantified: holding NWC at the FY2025 ratio cuts FY2026E FCFF from +Rp70.6bn to about -Rp8bn, floors the base case at zero and moves the target to about Rp8, so the conclusion is unchanged.

challenges.challenge: Weight 1.0 on DCF against the house primary-plus-two-cross-checks. The only cross-check with a positive denominator, P/B 0.63x on forecast book, implies about the Rp33 price and is dismissed with "a justified price-to-book is negative when ROE is below COE", which is not the right test when book is half a market-valued portfolio. No operating P/B ex the Rp261.1bn portfolio is shown and no peer comps are used.
challenges.answer: Added the operating-book cross-check: Rp261.1bn of the Rp516.3bn book is the portfolio at market, so the operating book is the remainder, and the market capitalisation is above that remainder while the DCF values the operating business at Rp39.2bn [S9]. P/B on the whole book is therefore not a value test. DCF remains the only weighted method because every multiple has a negative or near-zero denominator; the divergence is reconciled in section 4 and the lint warning is disclosed in weights.changed.

challenges.challenge: WACC uses kd_pre_tax 9.45% (rf 7.45% plus a 2.0% corporate spread) while the effective interest cost is 6.5% (FY2025 interest Rp24.29bn on about Rp376bn debt; 9M2026 Rp16.38bn) and the model's own cost_of_debt driver is 7.0%. Beta is levered at D/E 0.94 = gross debt over the depressed Rp33 market cap, which is circular for a SELL. The sensitivity shows a ~0.9pp lower WACC lifts the DCF from Rp6.74 to about Rp8.9.
challenges.answer: cost_of_debt is now 6.5 percent (FY2025 interest Rp24.3bn on about Rp376bn of debt; 9M2026 Rp16.4bn) and a -1.1pp WACC adjustment reflects the gap between the house build at 9.45 percent and the rate actually paid [S8][S9]. The unlevered beta of 0.585 relevers to 1.01 at the book debt-to-equity of about 0.57 instead of 1.21 at the market ratio of 0.94, which is distorted by the collapsed market capitalisation against a debt-funded securities book. WACC is 11.2 percent before the adjustment and 10.1 percent after; section 4 states both bases.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of Rp1,051.2bn is 9M of Rp861.0bn plus Q4 of Rp190.2bn. Q3 actual revenue was Rp99.0bn (9M 861.0 less H1 762.0, S10), so Q4 is 1.92x Q3 while section 3 says "the fourth quarter runs at roughly the third quarter's volume". No seasonal source is given; a Q4 at Rp99-120bn cuts FY2026E revenue to Rp960-981bn and deepens the loss.
challenges.answer: Clean Q3 2026 revenue is Rp94.4bn (9M clean Rp897.8bn less H1 clean Rp803.4bn, from the segment notes) and the FY2026E build now puts Q4 at about that run-rate, giving revenue of Rp1,000.3bn and an operating loss of Rp51.0bn [S10][S9]. The Q4/Q3 ratio is therefore about 1.09x, not 1.92x, and the wording in section 3 matches the build.

challenges.challenge: The 16% NWC/revenue assumption against the FY2025 actual 23.7% (Rp286.7bn / Rp1,211.0bn) produces a Rp118.5bn one-off working-capital release in FY2026E, which is the only reason FCFF is +Rp51.3bn on an EBIT of -Rp76.7bn. The report never discloses the one-off or that most of it is already in the 30 Sep balance sheet.
challenges.answer: NWC is now 15.5 percent of sales, the 30 Sep 2026 actual (inventory Rp135.9bn plus third-party receivables Rp27.7bn less trade payables Rp9.2bn against FY2026E sales), not 16 percent [S9]. Section 3 says the release has largely already happened and section 4 says the FY2026E inflow is counted twice because the September bridge already reflects it. Holding NWC at the FY2025 ratio of about 23.4 percent takes FY2026E FCFF from +Rp70.6bn to about -Rp8bn and floors the base case at zero.

challenges.challenge: No scenario shocks the securities mark even though it is 82% of the Rp319.4bn market cap: all three runs keep the bridge at Rp261.1bn while the 9M2026 mark fell Rp36.9bn and MTDL is carried at Rp153.1bn against Rp182.1bn cost. The bear narrative ("the securities portfolio is consumed") and the bull narrative ("sells down part of the equity portfolio to repay bank debt") are not in the shocks.
challenges.answer: Partly modelled, fully disclosed. The scenario block can only shock a.* inputs, not the valuation bridge, so a mark shock cannot be run; section 5 now states that every scenario holds the portfolio at its September mark and quantifies the consequence: the portfolio is most of the market capitalisation, so a mark-down of the kind seen in 2025 exceeds the entire base-case equity value, and the bear case is already zero. The bull narrative partial portfolio sale is not in the shocks; its missing interest saving is about Rp9bn a year pre-tax, roughly Rp1.4 per share, which is a conservatism in the bull [S9].

challenges.challenge: FY2025 operating cash flow was +Rp105.95bn (F42; capex Rp3.97bn, so FCF +Rp102bn, 32% of market cap) and is never mentioned; the bearish reading rests on EBITDA alone. The bull's portfolio sale and debt cut would save about Rp9bn/yr pre-tax (Rp12bn dividends against about Rp21bn interest) but is not in the bull shocks, and the South Sumatra plant is valued at zero.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now carries FY2025 operating cash flow of Rp106bn and explains it as a receivables collection (Rp167.9bn to Rp27.7bn) against FY2024 and FY2023 outflows of Rp65.9bn and Rp62.2bn, and the 9M2026 inflow of Rp25.9bn [S8][S9]. The portfolio-sale interest saving is quantified at about Rp9bn a year. The Dailymeal and South Sumatra construction in progress of Rp43.1bn is inside the operating capex forecast with its earnings inside the terminal margin, so adding the sunk capex as a separate bridge asset would double count it [S9].

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says "gross margin stays near 6%" but the shocks are -2pp off a 6.5% FY2027E base (4.5%); the base is called "the FY2024 economics" but uses a 9.0% terminal margin against a clean FY2024 rice-segment margin of 6.38% (S8 p71) and a clean FY2025 8.0%; and the bull at Rp40 is +22% over Rp33, not "barely above the price".
challenges.answer: The base case now ends at a 9.2 percent gross margin, above the clean FY2025 8.54 percent and below the FY2022 peak 10.19 percent, and sections 3 and 5 call it the top of the company own range rather than FY2024 economics [S8][S9]. The bear shock of -2pp off a 7.2 percent FY2027E base leaves about 5.2 percent, close to the FY2026 5.8 percent, matching the narrative. The bull is worth Rp36.0 against the Rp33 price and is now described as barely above it.

challenges.challenge: Several load-bearing quotes do not support the fact: F8's quote ("Total 23.612.387.542 26.696.901.384") does not contain the 29.063bn used (the sum of PPE 23.612 plus investment property 5.451); F22's quote shows only the 16.351bn COGS depreciation allocation, not 21.797bn; free float 29.3% and insider 69.4% are cited S8/S0 but S0 is Yahoo with no float (the pack's IDX-registry source is not in fund record); "negative ROE in every year since FY2022" is at best ambiguous (FY2022 net profit +Rp1.797bn).
challenges.answer: D&A is now carried as component facts with direct quotes: FY2025 fixed-asset depreciation of Rp23.612bn plus investment-property depreciation of Rp5.451bn (F53) equals Rp29.063bn, and 9M2026 Rp16.351bn of the COGS allocation plus Rp1.530bn of G&A plus Rp4.158bn of investment property (F54 and F55) equals Rp22.039bn [S8 notes 10 and 11; S9 notes 10, 11 and 26].
